decision.explanation: Reversing the limits gives ∫₀³ f(t) dt = ⟨-5, 1, 2⟩. The constant vector integrates to 3⟨-1, 1, -1⟩ = ⟨-3, 3, -3⟩. Adding gives ⟨-8, 4, -1⟩.

after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨5,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)+⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{3}⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+{⟨-t,\,t,\,-t⟩|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+⟨-3,\,3,\,-3⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-8,\,4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Given that 
${\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t=4\,i-2\,j+k,$ 
$c=u\,i-2\,j-2\,k,$
and 
${\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ what is the value of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(u\,i-2\,j-2\,k)\cdot (4\,i-2\,j+\,k) \\  & =4u+4-2 \\  & =4u+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $4u+2=0,$ which means that $u=-\frac{1}{2}.$
